item.title: Sounds, Alphabet, and Greetings
item.description: Lesson 1: Sounds, Alphabet, and Greetings Italian spelling is unusually regular: once you learn how letters sound, you can read most words aloud with confidence. The alphabet has 21 letters in common use, with j, k, w, x, and y appearing mainly in borrowed words. The five vowels — a, e, i, o, u —…

item.title: Essere, Avere, and Describing Yourself
item.description: Lesson 2: Essere, Avere, and Describing Yourself Two verbs carry most beginner conversation: essere (to be) and avere (to have). Italian verbs change their endings for each person, so the subject pronoun is often dropped: sono already means "I am," and ho already means "I have." Learn the full…

item.title: Regular Verbs in the Present Tense
item.description: Lesson 3: Regular Verbs in the Present Tense Italian verbs fall into three conjugations, identified by their infinitive endings: -are (parlare, to speak), -ere (vedere, to see), and -ire (partire, to leave; finire, to finish). Regular verbs follow predictable endings, and learning one model verb…

item.title: Articles, Nouns, and Gender
item.description: Lesson 4: Articles, Nouns, and Gender Every Italian noun has a gender — masculine or feminine — and number, and the article must match both. item.title: The Past Tense — Passato Prossimo
item.description: Lesson 5: The Past Tense — Passato Prossimo Italian tells completed past actions mainly with the passato prossimo, formed with the present of avere or essere plus the past participle. item.title: Food, Ordering, and Quantities
item.description: Lesson 6: Food, Ordering, and Quantities Food vocabulary is both practical and culturally rich, and ordering in Italy rewards politeness and a few set phrases. item.title: Future, Plans, and the Weather
item.description: Lesson 7: Future, Plans, and the Weather The future tense in Italian is formed from the infinitive, with endings added directly: for -are verbs, the a of the infinitive changes to e (parlare → parler-), and for -ere and -ire verbs the stem stays close to the infinitive. item.description: Lesson 8: Travel, Directions, and Everyday Conversation Travel Italian brings together everything so far: polite requests, numbers, directions, and past and future tenses.
